segment:
This is going to be one of those things. She knew how it would feel for these three men if she said anything about that out loud; the woman’s disappearance into her role was part of what allowed the other three to remain visible and present, to relax and talk like themselves.

The man with the glass walked around to his right to shake Mara’s hand too, and she turned with him—but she felt herself turning. This was going to be one of those things too. The conversation in her ear, the two men walking forward from either side to meet her there. The social expectations that surrounded her, how her face had looked when the door opened, the smile they were waiting for…

And suddenly the social world she found herself in had been pulled out of thin air, a little magical stage that someone else was setting up for her as she arrived and took center stage. The world would vanish behind her if she walked away; a world not made by her or anyone’s conscious will, just assembled by habit or convention, with no choice but to let the expectations gather around her face and body—but it was happening anyway.

She could walk away.
She didn’t want to.
This was the world she was in, right now, in front of these two men. What would it look like from outside?

A voice called her name again: Adrian’s.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

And that was when a door opened down the hallway behind her, releasing two voices into the room. One female, one male; one asking a question, the other replying; neither loud nor excited, just casual conversation. Jonah released her hand and turned away to look down the hall at them.
When Mara heard the voices and followed his gaze, she saw one young man who wasn’t Jonah, but close in size and shape; he had brown hair and a beard and was carrying a glass.

The brown-haired man glanced once over his shoulder, saw them standing there, nodded hello, and stepped right into the gathering, holding up his glass of wine—a half-full plastic cup with the Fulcrum logo on it. “Cheers.” He set it on the table against the wall to the left of the door, and stepped forward to shake Jonah’s hand as they exchanged names.

As he set down the glass and moved out of its space, a previously unseen catering worker entered from the hallway behind him and retrieved it. She wore the same black-and-white striped Fulcrum uniform shirt, though she looked old enough to have had that job since the Institute was founded; and she gave no outward sign of the social fact that she was taking their discarded drink back to the kitchen, while the rest of the conversation went on.

Mara watched this woman return to the hallway where she belonged, and noticed herself noticing who assumed whose labor.

This is going to be one of those things. She knew how it would feel for these three men if she said anything about that out loud; the woman’s disappearance into her role was part of what allowed the other three to remain visible and present, to relax and talk like themselves.

The man with the glass walked around to his right to shake Mara’s hand too, and she turned with him—but she felt herself turning. This was going to be one of those things too. The conversation in her ear, the two men walking forward from either side to meet her there. The social expectations that surrounded her, how her face had looked when the door opened, the smile they were waiting for…

And suddenly the social world she found herself in had been pulled out of thin air, a little magical stage that someone else was setting up for her as she arrived and took center stage. The world would vanish behind her if she walked away; a world not made by her or anyone’s conscious will, just assembled by habit or convention, with no choice but to let the expectations gather around her face and body—but it was happening anyway.

She could walk away.
She didn’t want to.
This was the world she was in, right now, in front of these two men. What would it look like from outside?

A voice called her name again: Adrian’s.

segment:
It wasn’t anything the woman herself had done, but an observation about space and motion and responsibility. Not just that everyone knew this glass was finished with, and that someone needed to take it away—which she already knew. But also that the invisible pattern of order-taking was so smooth here that no one could really deny having seen her do it. They were all witnesses to each other’s invisible labor, and the silence that followed it. She noticed how her own mind went along with that expectation of silence, even as she wished for something different—wishing she were able to find another way to be here, without adding to this pattern of who sees and who is unseen, who is acknowledged and who is taken for granted.
 

The brown-haired man finished exchanging names, and shook Mara’s hand in turn. His name was Adrian, and he seemed to notice how long it took her to reply; he kept his grip and waited while she found words to say.
“I’m really glad to be here,” she said, her hand still in his. “Thank you.”

Adrian smiled and released her hand, then turned his gaze to something she wasn’t quite sure he was seeing yet.
“So what did they say at your interview?” He gestured casually toward the back of the room, where a second glass had just been placed on the same table—the brown-haired man’s empty beer bottle, retrieved by someone Mara hadn’t even seen enter, a younger woman in black-and-white stripes. She seemed to be holding back for some reason, hanging behind Adrian’s right shoulder as he took stock of the other two people in the room.

segment:
She realized it was the first time she had seen any servant class here, other than the chef and staff; and she tried to imagine how often someone of a different station must have served her food, collected her garbage, and washed her laundry at some point over the years without her full awareness. She didn’t try to make an estimate, knowing that it wouldn’t be accurate. But she decided that she would never underestimate it again.

The young man with the brown beard and the glass of wine turned his attention to Mara, grinning in an almost identical manner as he shook her hand; she shook it back, and realized she must not yet have relaxed her own face, because he was still giving her a wide smile after their names were exchanged. “Hello, I’m Adrian,” he said again.

“You are?” Mara echoed, now feeling like she might be about to smile too. She hoped not.
“That is to say, I’m Adrian. Pleased to meet you.” He let go of her hand and leaned back to give a sweeping gesture to the room in which they now all stood. “Welcome to Fulcrum!”
Mara found herself smiling now. “Thank you.”
Adrian was still standing right in front of her, and it occurred to Mara that it was probably up to her to step out of the way for her own sake at this point. But instead, she just waited for him to do it.
